formats.name: Email
formats.summary: Short, clear and polite, with a subject line that says what it is about.
layout: To: the person's email address.
Subject: a few words that say what the email is about, such as "Volunteer application for Panda Week".
A greeting on its own line.
Short paragraphs, one main point each.
A sign-off and your name (in practice tasks, use a made-up name).
formats.opening: Say who you are and why you are writing in the first one or two sentences. For example: "I am writing to apply for a place as a Panda Week volunteer."
formats.closing: Say what you would like to happen next, then sign off. For example: "I look forward to hearing from you. Kind regards,"
formats.tone: If you don't know the person, keep it formal: "Dear Mr Patel", no slang, no text-speak, no emojis. If you know them well, you can be friendlier, but still use full sentences.
checklist: I included a subject line.
I started with a greeting, such as "Dear ...".
My first paragraph says why I am writing.
I used a new paragraph for each main point.
I ended with what I want to happen next.
I signed off, such as "Kind regards" and a name.

questions.prompt: You are emailing someone you have never met. Which opening is best?
options: Dear Mr Patel, I am writing to ask about volunteering at Panda Week.
To whoever reads this, I want to volunteer.
questions.why: It uses a formal greeting and says straight away why you are writing. The others are too casual for someone you don't know.

questions.prompt: What should the subject line of an email do?
options: Stay blank so the reader opens it
Say in a few words what the email is about
questions.why: A good subject line tells the reader at a glance why you are writing, for example "Volunteer application for Panda Week".

questions.prompt: Which sentence is best for explaining why you are writing?
options: I am writing to apply for the weekend job advertised on your website.
This email is an email about a job.
questions.why: It says clearly who you are writing about and why, in a polite, formal way.

questions.prompt: Which closing and sign-off suits an email to someone you have never met?
options: Kind regards, followed by your name
questions.why: "Kind regards" is polite without being stiff. The others are too casual or too personal for a stranger.

questions.prompt: Which request is the politest?
options: You need to tell me how much it is.
Could you please let me know the cost of a group ticket?
questions.why: "Could you please" is polite and clear. The others sound abrupt or bossy.

questions.prompt: What should each paragraph of an email usually do?
options: Cover every point in one big block
questions.why: One main point per paragraph makes an email easy to follow.

questions.prompt: What should you do before you press send?
options: Read it through and check spelling and punctuation
Delete the greeting to save time
Write it all in capital letters
questions.why: Proof-reading catches mistakes and makes a better impression.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the best way to ask for a reply?
options: Reply when you feel like it.
I would be grateful for a reply by Friday 12 June.
questions.why: It is polite and gives a clear date.

questions.prompt: Which greeting suits a friendly email to a friend?
questions.why: A friend can be greeted by first name. The other greetings are formal.

questions.prompt: Which is the best order for an email of application?
options: Greeting, reason for writing, details, polite close, sign-off
Sign-off, details, greeting, reason for writing
Details, greeting, sign-off, reason for writing
Reason for writing, sign-off, greeting, details
questions.why: A reader expects to be greeted first, told why you are writing, given the details, and then thanked.

formats.name: Formal letter
formats.summary: Like a formal email, but with addresses and a date.
layout: Your address in the top right corner.
The date underneath your address.
The other person's name or job title and address on the left, a little lower.
A greeting: "Dear Ms Khan" if you know the name, "Dear Sir or Madam" if you don't.
Paragraphs, then a sign-off and your name.
formats.opening: State your purpose clearly: "I am writing to complain about ..." or "I am writing to ask for ..."
formats.closing: Use "Yours sincerely" if you used their name, and "Yours faithfully" if you wrote "Dear Sir or Madam".
formats.tone: Formal and polite, even when you are complaining. Explain calmly, give reasons, and suggest what should happen.
checklist: I included my address and the date.
I included the other person's name or job title and address.
My greeting and sign-off match (sincerely or faithfully).
My first paragraph says why I am writing.
I stayed polite throughout.

questions.prompt: You started your letter with "Dear Sir or Madam". How should you sign off?
questions.why: When you don't know the person's name, you use "Yours faithfully". "Yours sincerely" goes with a named person, such as "Dear Ms Khan".

questions.prompt: You know the person's name and start with "Dear Ms Khan". How should you sign off?
questions.why: When you use a name, you sign off with "Yours sincerely". "Yours faithfully" goes with "Dear Sir or Madam".

questions.prompt: Where does your own address go in a formal letter?
options: At the bottom of the page
questions.why: The sender's address goes at the top right, with the date underneath.

questions.prompt: Where does the date go?
questions.why: The date goes under the sender's address near the top.

questions.prompt: Which first sentence suits a letter of complaint?
options: I am writing to complain about the coach trip that was cancelled on 14 May.
questions.why: It states the purpose clearly and politely, with a date.

questions.prompt: Which sentence keeps a complaint polite but firm?
options: I would be grateful if you could refund my fare in full.
Give me my money back now.
I demand a refund immediately, or else.
You had better sort this out.
questions.why: It makes a clear request without being rude.

questions.prompt: What should the last paragraph of a formal letter usually do?
options: Say what you want to happen and thank the reader
questions.why: Ending with a clear request and a thank-you leaves the reader knowing what to do next.

questions.prompt: Which greeting is correct if you do not know the person's name?
questions.why: "Dear Sir or Madam" is the standard formal greeting when you do not have a name.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is too informal for a formal letter?
options: I was totally gutted about it.
I would like to explain what happened.
questions.why: "Totally gutted" is slang. A formal letter uses a more measured phrase such as "extremely disappointed".

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a formal register?
options: I should be grateful for a reply within fourteen days.
questions.why: It is polite, precise and fully formal.

formats.name: Article
formats.summary: For a newsletter, magazine or website. It needs a headline and should grab the reader.
layout: A headline that is short and catches attention.
A subheading (optional) that adds a little more detail.
Paragraphs. You can use subheadings to break up a longer article.
Your name as the writer (a by-line) is optional.
formats.opening: Hook the reader. You could ask a question, give a surprising fact (from the task), or describe a scene. Then make it clear what the article is about.
formats.closing: End with a memorable final thought or a call to action, such as "So next Monday, leave the car at home and catch the bus."
formats.tone: Match the readers. For students you can be lively and direct ("you"), but keep it in full sentences without slang.
checklist: I wrote a headline.
My opening hooks the reader.
I used paragraphs, and subheadings if it is long.
I spoke to the reader directly where it helps.
I ended with a strong final thought or call to action.

questions.prompt: Which is the best headline for a college newsletter article encouraging students to use buses?
options: Get On Board: Why the Bus Beats the School Run
This article is about buses and why you should use them more often than you do now
questions.why: It is short, catches attention and hints at the article's point. The others are too plain or too long.

questions.prompt: What is the job of the opening paragraph of an article?
options: List every fact in the article
Hook the reader and show what the article is about
questions.why: A good opening grabs attention and tells readers what to expect.

questions.prompt: Which opening is best for an article about healthy eating?
options: I will now write about food and stuff.
Have you ever wondered why a packed lunch can beat a canteen meal?
questions.why: A question speaks to the reader and makes them want to read on.

questions.prompt: Why do articles often use subheadings?
options: They break up the text and help readers find sections
They must always be full sentences
questions.why: Subheadings make an article easier to scan and follow.

questions.prompt: Which ending suits a persuasive article?
options: So next Monday, leave the car at home and give the bus a try.
I have run out of things to say.
Thank you for reading my homework.
questions.why: A call to action leaves the reader with something to do.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses direct address?
options: People may be surprised how much money could be saved.
Money can be saved by some.
You may be surprised how much money you could save.
questions.why: Direct address speaks straight to the reader with "you".

questions.prompt: Which of these is a rhetorical question?
options: What time does the bus leave?
How much is a day ticket?
Who wants to sit in traffic for an hour every morning?
questions.why: A rhetorical question is asked for effect, and the writer expects the answer to be "nobody".

questions.prompt: Which tone suits an article for students?
options: Lively and friendly, in full sentences
questions.why: A lively, friendly tone keeps readers interested, while full sentences keep it correct.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to support a point in an article?
options: Give a reason and an example or fact
questions.why: Reasons and evidence make a point convincing.

questions.prompt: Which set of features belongs in an article for a college newsletter?
options: A postal address and the date
A headline, paragraphs and a clear ending
questions.why: A headline, paragraphs and an ending are the basic features of an article.

formats.name: Review
formats.summary: Your opinion of something, with reasons, to help other people decide.
layout: A title that names what you are reviewing.
A star rating or score (optional).
Paragraphs: what it is, what was good, what was not so good.
A final recommendation.
formats.opening: Say what you are reviewing and give a quick first impression: "I visited Hollins Park with my family last weekend, and it was better than I expected."
formats.closing: Give a clear recommendation and who it would suit: "I'd recommend it to families with young children, but go early."
formats.tone: Friendly and honest. Give reasons and examples for every opinion, not just "it was good".
checklist: I named what I am reviewing.
I gave good points with reasons.
I gave at least one thing that could be better.
I ended with a clear recommendation.

questions.prompt: Which sentence would work best in a review?
options: The feeding talk was the highlight, because the keeper answered every question from the children.
Everything was bad and nobody should go.
questions.why: It gives an opinion and a reason with a specific example, which helps the reader decide.

questions.prompt: What should the first paragraph of a review do?
options: Say what you are reviewing and give a first impression
questions.why: Readers need to know what is being reviewed and what you thought, straight away.

questions.prompt: Which comment is balanced?
options: The café was perfect in every way.
The café was friendly, although the prices were high.
questions.why: It gives a good point and a not-so-good point.

questions.prompt: What should a good recommendation include?
options: Who it would suit and why
A question for the reader's teacher
questions.why: Telling readers who would enjoy it helps them decide.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives a reason?
options: I enjoyed it because the guide made every dish easy to understand.
questions.why: "Because" shows the reason behind the opinion.

questions.prompt: Which comment is the most helpful to someone deciding whether to go?
options: Tickets cost £12, but the queue at lunchtime lasted forty minutes.
questions.why: It gives specific facts a reader can act on.

questions.prompt: Which critical comment is fair and helpful?
options: The seats were uncomfortable, so I would bring a cushion.
questions.why: It gives the problem and a useful tip.

questions.prompt: Which tone is best for a review?
questions.why: Readers trust honest opinions that come with reasons.

questions.prompt: Which is the best final sentence for a review?
options: Overall, I would recommend it for families, but go early to avoid queues.
questions.why: It sums up the view, says who it suits and gives a tip.

questions.prompt: Which group of words shows the writer's opinion?
questions.why: Opinion words describe how good or bad something was.

formats.name: Report
formats.summary: Information and recommendations for a group, laid out in clear sections.
layout: A title that says what the report is about.
To, From and Date lines (optional, but useful).
An introduction that says why the report was written.
Subheadings for each section.
A final section called "Recommendations" or "Conclusion".
formats.opening: Explain the purpose: "This report looks at what there is for young people in Hawsden and Brayminster, and suggests ways to improve it."
formats.closing: Give clear recommendations. Numbered points work well: "1. Run a later bus on Fridays."
formats.tone: Formal and factual. Avoid "I think" in most of it. Save opinions for the recommendations, and explain them.
checklist: I gave the report a title.
My introduction explains the purpose.
I used subheadings for each section.
I kept the tone formal and factual.
I finished with clear recommendations.

questions.prompt: Which subheading suits a formal report?
questions.why: Report subheadings should be short and plain, so the reader can find each section quickly.

questions.prompt: What does the introduction of a report do?
options: Explains the purpose of the report
questions.why: A report starts by saying why it was written.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is suited to a formal report?
options: It was found that most students travel to college by bus.
Loads of students go by bus lol.
Basically everyone is on the bus.
questions.why: A report uses a formal, factual tone.

questions.prompt: Where do recommendations usually go in a report?
options: In the middle of the introduction
In a final section, often as numbered points
questions.why: Recommendations come last, after the findings.

questions.prompt: Which is a clear recommendation?
options: The council should install a covered cycle store by the main entrance.
questions.why: It says who should do what, and where.

questions.prompt: The survey found that 18 out of 40 students use the bus. Which sentence reports this best?
options: Nearly half of the students (18 out of 40) travel by bus.
questions.why: A good report turns figures into a clear sentence.

questions.prompt: Which should be avoided in a formal report?
questions.why: Slang and chat do not suit a formal report.

questions.prompt: Which opening line suits a report for a head teacher?
options: This report describes how Panda Day went and suggests improvements for next year.
questions.why: It states the purpose formally and clearly.

questions.prompt: Which heading fits a section about what went wrong?
questions.why: Headings should be short, plain and informative.

questions.prompt: What are the "To", "From" and "Date" lines at the top of a report for?
options: To make the page look full
To show who it is for, who wrote it and when
questions.why: They tell the reader the basic facts about the report.

formats.name: Blog post
formats.summary: A personal, chatty piece for a website, with a clear view.
layout: A title that catches attention.
Short paragraphs, which are easier to read on a screen.
Subheadings or a list are fine if they help.
formats.opening: Start in a personal way, such as a question or a short story, and make your view clear early on.
formats.closing: Sum up your view and invite readers to respond: "Where would you rather live? Let me know in the comments."
formats.tone: Personal and friendly ("I", "you"), but still in full sentences with accurate spelling and punctuation. No text-speak.
checklist: I wrote a title.
My opening is personal and makes my view clear.
I used short paragraphs.
I gave reasons for my view.
I ended by summing up or inviting a response.

questions.prompt: Which is the best final sentence for a blog post?
options: So that's why I'd pick a village every time. Would you? Tell me in the comments.
That's all I have to say about towns and villages and stuff.
questions.why: It sums up the writer's view and invites the reader to respond, which suits a blog.

questions.prompt: Which title would catch a reader's attention?
options: I Moved from a Village to a Town: Here's What Surprised Me
questions.why: A good title is specific and makes you want to read on.

questions.prompt: Why does a blog post use short paragraphs?
options: They are easier to read on a screen
questions.why: Short paragraphs stop the page looking like a solid block of text.

questions.prompt: Which opening is personal and clear?
options: Moving is a thing that people do.
In this blog post the following will be explained.
Last month I swapped fields for pavements, and I have a lot to say about it.
questions.why: It sounds like a real person and tells you what is coming.

questions.prompt: Which tone is right for a blog?
options: Friendly and honest, in full sentences
questions.why: A blog can be personal, but it should still be clear and correct.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives a reason for a view?
options: I prefer the town because I can reach my friends on foot.
questions.why: "Because" introduces a reason.

questions.prompt: Which closing invites readers to join in?
options: That is my last word and nobody can change it.
What do you think? Tell me in the comments.
questions.why: Ending with a question encourages readers to respond.

questions.prompt: Which is a good way to add interest to a blog post?
options: A short story about something that happened to you
questions.why: Personal stories bring a blog to life.

questions.prompt: Which should you avoid in a blog post?
questions.why: Text-speak looks careless, even in a friendly post.

questions.prompt: Which ending is balanced and honest?
options: I miss the quiet, but I would not go back.
questions.why: It admits something good about the old place while being clear about the choice.

formats.name: Web forum post
formats.summary: A short post on an online discussion board that gives your view and invites replies.
layout: A clear title or subject line, if the board asks for one.
A friendly start, such as "Hi everyone", or straight into your view.
Short paragraphs, because posts are read on screens.
Your view first, then your reasons and a short example.
A question or invitation to reply at the end.
formats.opening: State your view straight away: "I think buses should be free for under-18s, and here are my reasons."
formats.closing: Invite a reply: "What do you think? Has anyone else tried this?"
formats.tone: Chatty and friendly, but still in full sentences with correct spelling and punctuation. No text-speak or emojis, and stay polite even when you disagree.
checklist: I gave my view in the first sentence or two.
I gave at least two reasons.
I included an example or a short story.
I used short paragraphs.
I finished by inviting replies.
I kept the tone friendly but polite.

questions.prompt: Which is the best first sentence for a forum post giving your view on later school start times?
options: Hi everyone, I think school should start later, and I have three reasons.
school start times r bad lol
Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to complain.
questions.why: It says what the writer thinks straight away, sounds friendly and uses full words. The others are too casual, too formal for a forum, or say nothing.

questions.prompt: Where in a forum post should your view appear?
options: In the very last line only
In the first sentence or two
questions.why: Readers should know your view straight away.

questions.prompt: Which reply to a question is the most helpful?
options: I'd say yes, because the guided tour answers questions you would otherwise miss.
questions.why: It gives a view and a reason.

questions.prompt: How can you disagree politely?
options: I see your point, but I think evening buses matter more.
questions.why: It acknowledges the other view before giving yours.

questions.prompt: A good forum post usually ends with...
options: A question or an invitation to reply
questions.why: Inviting a reply keeps the discussion going.

questions.prompt: Which tone suits a web forum?
options: Friendly and chatty, but still clear
questions.why: A forum is informal, but readers still need to understand you.

questions.prompt: Which sentence includes an example?
options: For example, last winter my bus was cancelled three times in a week.
questions.why: A specific example makes a point real.

questions.prompt: Why are short paragraphs useful in a forum post?
options: They are quicker to type backwards
They are required by the website
They are easier to read on a screen
questions.why: Short paragraphs keep a post readable.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT suitable in a forum post?
questions.why: Capital letters look like shouting and make a post harder to read.

questions.prompt: Which opening shows you are replying to another member?
options: Hi Dani, I agree with your point about late buses.
questions.why: It names the person and links to what they said.

formats.name: Online form
formats.summary: A box on a website where you give your views to an organisation. Be clear, polite and to the point.
layout: Read the label on each box before you write.
Write in full sentences, even in a small box.
Keep each answer to the question in that box.
Give a reason and a short example.
Check your spelling before you press submit.
formats.opening: Answer the question in the box straight away: "The part I enjoyed most was the tasting stop at the market."
formats.closing: Finish with a polite line: "Thank you for asking for my views."
formats.tone: Polite, clear and fairly formal, as if you were writing to a company or a council.
checklist: I answered the question in the box.
I gave a reason for each view.
I included an example.
I wrote in full sentences.
I stayed polite, even when giving criticism.
I thanked them at the end.

questions.prompt: A box asks "What did you like most?" Which answer is best?
options: The guide was friendly and explained each dish, which made the tour more interesting.
I did not like it at all.
questions.why: It answers the question and gives a reason. "It was good" gives the reader nothing to use.

questions.prompt: What should you do first when you reach a box on an online form?
options: Read the label on the box
questions.why: The label tells you what to write.

questions.prompt: Which answer is best for the box "What could be improved?"
options: The group was large, so a smaller group would make it easier to hear the guide.
questions.why: It gives a clear point, a reason and a suggestion.

questions.prompt: Why should you write in full sentences on a form?
options: They make your meaning clear to the reader
questions.why: A reader who is not in front of you needs clear sentences.

questions.prompt: Which is a polite way to complain on a form?
options: I was disappointed that the tour started late, and I would appreciate a smaller group next time.
questions.why: It is honest, polite and constructive.

questions.prompt: A box asks "Would you recommend this?" Which answer is best?
options: Yes, I would, especially for families, because the guide was friendly and the food was excellent.
Maybe if I feel like it.
questions.why: It gives an answer, a reason and who it suits.

questions.prompt: What should you do before pressing submit?
questions.why: Proof-reading avoids mistakes.

questions.prompt: The box is small and you have a lot to say. What should you do?
options: Write very tiny so everything fits
Choose the most important points and write them clearly
questions.why: Clear, short answers are better than cramming.

questions.prompt: Which line suits the end of a feedback form?
options: Thank you for asking for my views.
questions.why: A polite thank-you is a good finish.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives a reason for a view?
options: I enjoyed the tasting stops because I tried foods I had never eaten before.
questions.why: "Because" shows the reason.

formats.name: Information or advice sheet
formats.summary: Clear, helpful guidance for readers, with a heading and short sections or tips.
layout: A title that says who the advice is for.
A short introduction saying why the advice helps.
Subheadings or numbered tips.
Each tip says what to do, and why.
A short closing line.
formats.opening: Say who the advice is for and why it helps: "If you are travelling by train for the first time, these tips will save you time and worry."
formats.closing: End with a reassuring line or repeat the most important tip: "Remember: buy your ticket before you board."
formats.tone: Helpful and direct. Use "you" and short sentences, and give simple instructions.
checklist: My title says who the advice is for.
I wrote a short introduction.
I used subheadings or numbered tips.
Each tip says what to do and why.
I used simple, direct language.
I ended with a reminder or a reassuring line.

questions.prompt: Which is the best subheading for an advice sheet about first train journeys?
options: Why trains are great and I love them so much
Buy your ticket before you board
questions.why: It tells the reader exactly what to do. The others are too vague or too long, or are about the writer rather than the reader.

questions.prompt: Which title shows who an advice sheet is for?
options: Your First Train Journey: Tips for Travelling Alone
questions.why: A good title says who the advice is for and what it covers.

questions.prompt: Which tip explains what to do and why?
options: Charge your phone the night before, so you can show your ticket on the screen.
questions.why: A tip with a reason is more helpful and more convincing.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses direct, simple language?
options: It might be advisable that early arrival be considered in the context of platform location.
Maybe get there at some time.
Arrive ten minutes early so that you can find the right platform.
questions.why: Advice should be clear and direct.

questions.prompt: When are numbered tips the best choice?
options: When the order of the steps matters
When you want to hide the order
When there is only one tip
questions.why: Numbers show a sequence.

questions.prompt: Which is a good opening line for an advice sheet?
options: I am a person who walks.
If you are walking in the desert for the first time, these tips will keep you safe and comfortable.
questions.why: It says who the advice is for and why it helps.

questions.prompt: Which closing line reassures the reader?
options: Good luck, you will need it.
Follow these steps and you will be fine, and staff are always happy to help.
questions.why: A reassuring ending leaves the reader feeling confident.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is written as an instruction?
options: The timetable could have been checked.
Check the timetable before you leave.
questions.why: Instructions use the base form of the verb and speak to the reader.

questions.prompt: Which heading is the clearest?
questions.why: A clear heading tells the reader what is in the section.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is too vague to be good advice?
options: Carry at least two litres of water.
Wear a hat and sun cream.
Be careful and do things properly.
questions.why: Good advice is specific, so the reader knows exactly what to do.

formats.name: Diary entry
formats.summary: Personal writing about what happened and how you felt.
layout: The day and date at the top.
Events in the order they happened.
Your feelings and thoughts, not only the facts.
Something you learned or noticed.
A look ahead at the end.
formats.opening: Start with the date and a line that sets the scene: "Saturday 14 June. Today was the longest and best day of the whole trip."
formats.closing: End with a thought about the day or what comes next: "I can't wait to go back tomorrow."
formats.tone: Personal and chatty, in the first person ("I"), but still in full sentences with correct punctuation.
checklist: I put the day and date at the top.
I described events in order.
I said how I felt.
I included a detail that only someone there would notice.
I said what I learned.
I looked ahead at the end.

questions.prompt: Which sentence belongs in a diary entry?
options: I felt nervous when the bus was late, but it all worked out in the end.
questions.why: A diary says what happened and how the writer felt. The other lines belong in a notice, a formal letter or small print.

questions.prompt: How should a diary entry usually start?
options: With the day and the date
questions.why: The date shows when the events happened.

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows feelings?
options: The keeper opened the gate at nine.
I was nervous when the keeper opened the gate, but I soon relaxed.
questions.why: A diary says how the writer felt, not only what happened.

questions.prompt: Which sentence keeps events in the order they happened?
options: First we fed the animals, then we cleaned the garden, and after lunch we watched a talk.
After lunch we watched a talk, first we fed the animals, then we cleaned the garden.
questions.why: A diary usually follows time order.

questions.prompt: Which person is a diary written in?
questions.why: A diary is a personal record, so it uses "I".

questions.prompt: Which is a good descriptive detail?
options: The bamboo smelled like fresh-cut grass.
questions.why: Specific detail makes writing vivid.

questions.prompt: Which ending looks ahead?
options: Tomorrow I am helping the keepers with the afternoon feed, and I can't wait.
questions.why: Looking ahead is a natural way to finish a diary.

questions.prompt: Which tone suits a diary entry?
options: Personal and chatty, in full sentences
questions.why: A diary sounds like the writer, but should still be written in correct sentences.

questions.prompt: Which of these does NOT belong in a diary entry?
questions.why: "Yours faithfully" is the ending of a formal letter.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the past tense correctly?
options: We arrive at eight and the keepers was already working.
We arrives at eight and the keepers were already working.
We arriving at eight and the keepers is already working.
We arrived at eight and the keepers were already working.
questions.why: A diary about today usually uses the past tense, with correct verbs.

formats.name: Newsletter
formats.summary: A short update for a group, with a title, headings and a friendly, informative tone.
layout: The name of the newsletter and the date or issue.
A short welcome saying what is inside.
Headings for each item.
Short paragraphs.
Dates and contact details at the end.
formats.opening: Welcome readers and say what is inside: "Welcome to this month's newsletter. Read on for news about the summer fair and our new bus service."
formats.closing: Remind readers of the next date or how to get involved: "Come along on 12 July, and bring a friend."
formats.tone: Friendly and positive, speaking to the group as "we" and "you".
checklist: I gave the newsletter a name.
I started with a short welcome.
I used a heading for each item.
I wrote short paragraphs.
I spoke to the readers as "you".
I ended with a date or a way to get involved.

questions.prompt: Which is the best heading for a village newsletter item about a summer fair?
options: Summer Fair: Come and Join Us on 12 July!
An event that is going to happen in the future in the village hall
questions.why: It says what the item is about, gives the date and invites people. The others are too short, too long or too vague.

questions.prompt: What goes at the top of a newsletter?
options: The name of the newsletter and the date
questions.why: Readers want to know what it is and when it is from.

questions.prompt: Which welcome works best?
options: Welcome to this month's newsletter. Read on for news about the summer fair and our new bus service.
questions.why: It welcomes readers and tells them what is inside.

questions.prompt: Why use a heading for each item?
options: Readers can scan and find what interests them
questions.why: Headings make a newsletter easy to scan.

questions.prompt: Which tone suits a newsletter?
options: Friendly and positive, speaking to "you" and "we"
questions.why: A newsletter builds a sense of community.

questions.prompt: Which closing line works well?
options: Come along on 12 July and bring a friend.
questions.why: It gives a date and invites people to join in.

questions.prompt: Which is best for event details?
options: The date, time and place in a short list
questions.why: Event details should be easy to find.

questions.prompt: Which heading is best for news of a bus timetable change?
questions.why: It is specific and tells the reader what and when.

questions.prompt: Which sentence invites people to get involved?
options: If you would like to help at the fair, please speak to Maya at the village hall.
questions.why: It says what to do and who to ask.

questions.prompt: Which does NOT belong in a newsletter item?
questions.why: A newsletter should be friendly and respectful.

spag.name: Full stops and capital letters
explain: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop (or a question mark or exclamation mark).
Use capital letters for names of people, places, days and months, and for "I".
If you have two complete sentences, don't join them with a comma. Use a full stop instead.

example.wrong: the bus was late, we missed the start.
example.right: The bus was late. We missed the start.

questions.prompt: Which is punctuated correctly?
options: we went to tel aviv in may.
We went to tel aviv in may.
We went to Tel Aviv in may
We went to Tel Aviv in May.
questions.why: The sentence starts with a capital, "Tel Aviv" and "May" are names so they need capitals, and it ends with a full stop.

questions.prompt: Which pair of sentences is punctuated correctly?
options: The bus was late. We missed the start.
The bus was late, we missed the start.
The bus was late we missed the start.
the bus was late. We missed the start.
questions.why: Two complete sentences need a full stop between them, and each starts with a capital letter. A comma is not strong enough.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has the right capital letters?
options: On friday we visit the zoo.
On Friday we visit The zoo.
On Friday we visit the zoo.
on Friday we visit the zoo.
questions.why: Days of the week need capitals, and so does the first word of a sentence, but not "the" in the middle.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses "I" correctly?
options: Yesterday i went to the market.
yesterday I went to the market.
Yesterday, i went to the market.
Yesterday I went to the market.
questions.why: "I" is always a capital letter.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly for names?
options: maya lives in brayminster, near northcaster.
Maya lives in Brayminster, near Northcaster.
Maya lives in brayminster, near Northcaster.
Maya Lives In Brayminster, Near Northcaster.
questions.why: Names of people and places start with capitals. Other words in the sentence do not.

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
options: I love pandas. They eat bamboo all day.
I love pandas, they eat bamboo all day.
I love pandas they eat bamboo all day.
I love pandas. they eat bamboo all day.
questions.why: Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

questions.prompt: Which sentence ends correctly?
questions.why: A statement ends with a full stop.

questions.prompt: Which fixes the run-on sentence "The train was late the platform was empty"?
options: The train was late the platform. Was empty.
The train. Was late the platform was empty.
the train was late. the platform was empty.
The train was late. The platform was empty.
questions.why: There are two complete ideas, so they need a full stop between them and a capital letter on the second.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has the right capitals for days and months?
options: My birthday is on Tuesday 5 March.
My birthday is on tuesday 5 march.
My Birthday Is On Tuesday 5 March.
my birthday is on Tuesday 5 march.
questions.why: Days and months start with capital letters.

questions.prompt: Which line punctuates a list and two sentences correctly?
options: We saw lions, tigers and bears then. We had lunch.
We saw lions, tigers and bears. Then we had lunch.
We saw lions, tigers and bears. then we had lunch.
We saw lions tigers and bears. Then we had lunch.
questions.why: The list has commas, the first sentence ends with a full stop, and the next one starts with a capital letter.

spag.name: Question marks
explain: Use a question mark at the end of a direct question.
Questions often start with who, what, where, when, why, how, can, could, do or is.
In emails and letters, questions are a good way to ask for information politely.

example.wrong: Could you tell me what time the talk starts.
example.right: Could you tell me what time the talk starts?

questions.prompt: Which sentence needs a question mark at the end?
options: Is lunch included in the price
I would like to book two tickets
questions.why: "Is lunch included in the price" is asking something, so it ends with a question mark.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Could you tell me where the station is.
Could you tell me where the station is!
Could you tell me where the station is?
Could you tell me where the station is,
questions.why: It is a direct question, so it ends with a question mark.

questions.prompt: Which of these should NOT end with a question mark?
options: Can we bring our own lunch
I wonder when the tour starts
questions.why: "I wonder when the tour starts" is a statement about a question, not a direct question, so it ends with a full stop.

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
options: Why are the buses always late.
Why are the buses always late?
Why. Are the buses always late?
Why are the buses always late,
questions.why: A direct question ends with a question mark.

questions.prompt: Which request is the politest and punctuated correctly?
options: Would you mind telling me what time the tour starts?
Tell me what time the tour starts?
Would you mind telling me what time the tour starts.
questions.why: A polite request that asks a direct question ends with a question mark.

questions.prompt: Which question is written correctly for an email asking for information?
questions.why: It is a proper question with the verb first, and it ends with a question mark.

questions.prompt: Which tag question is punctuated correctly?
options: It's a long walk, isn't it.
It's a long walk isn't it?
It's a long walk? isn't it.
It's a long walk, isn't it?
questions.why: A tag question has a comma before it and a question mark at the end.

questions.prompt: Which pair is punctuated correctly?
options: Where do you live? How do you travel to college?
Where do you live? How do you travel to college.
Where do you live. How do you travel to college?
Where do you live? how do you travel to college?
questions.why: Each question ends with a question mark and the next one starts with a capital letter.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a question?
options: Floating in the Dead Sea is easy
Have you ever floated in the Dead Sea
I have floated in the Dead Sea
questions.why: Only the first asks something, so it needs a question mark.

questions.prompt: Which sentence should end with a full stop, not a question mark?
options: Does the bus run on Sundays
She asked whether the bus was running
questions.why: It reports a question rather than asking one directly.

spag.name: Exclamation marks
explain: Use an exclamation mark to show strong feeling, surprise or a command.
Use only one at a time, and not too often. In formal writing, you may not need any.
They work well in an article or a blog: "Leave the car at home!"

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an exclamation mark best?
options: I am writing to ask about tickets!
Try the bus for one week and see the difference!
questions.why: This is a call to action in a persuasive piece, so an exclamation mark adds energy. The others are formal phrases that should not have one.

questions.prompt: Which sentence suits an exclamation mark?
questions.why: Exclamation marks show strong feeling, such as delight or surprise.

questions.prompt: Which line uses exclamation marks sensibly?
questions.why: One exclamation mark is enough.

questions.prompt: What should a formal letter of complaint usually do about exclamation marks?
questions.why: A formal letter stays calm and measured.

questions.prompt: Which command suits an exclamation mark?
questions.why: A sudden warning or command is often followed by an exclamation mark.

questions.prompt: How many exclamation marks should you normally use at one time?
questions.why: A single exclamation mark makes the point. More looks careless.

questions.prompt: Which blog line uses an exclamation mark well?
options: We made it to the top, and the view was incredible!
Thank you for your letter of 3 May!
questions.why: It shows genuine excitement. The others are formal or neutral lines.

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows strong surprise?
options: I can't believe we found a free table!
questions.why: The words and the exclamation mark together show surprise.

questions.prompt: Which is punctuated correctly?
questions.why: It is an exclamation, so it ends with a single exclamation mark.

questions.prompt: In an article for students, which is the strongest call to action?
options: Give the bus a try this week!
The bus is a form of transport.
questions.why: It tells the reader what to do, with energy.

spag.name: Commas
explain: Use commas to separate items in a list: "falafel, hummus and salad". You usually don't need one before "and".
Use a comma after an opening word or phrase: "However, the bus was late." "In the morning, we went to the market."
Don't use a comma to join two full sentences.

example.wrong: We saw pandas monkeys and meerkats.
example.right: We saw pandas, monkeys and meerkats.

questions.prompt: Which is punctuated correctly?
options: After lunch we, walked to the beach.
After, lunch we walked to the beach.
After lunch we walked, to the beach.
After lunch, we walked to the beach.
questions.why: "After lunch" is an opening phrase, so the comma goes straight after it.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has the commas in the right place for a list?
options: We bought bread olives, cheese and, fruit.
We bought bread, olives, cheese and fruit.
We bought, bread olives cheese and fruit.
We bought bread, olives cheese, and fruit
questions.why: Commas separate the items in a list, and "and" joins the last two.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a comma correctly after an opening word?
questions.why: A comma follows an opening word such as "However".

questions.prompt: Which sentence has the comma in the right place?
options: When the bus arrived we, got on.
When, the bus arrived we got on.
When the bus arrived, we got on.
When the bus, arrived we got on.
questions.why: A comma follows the opening clause.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a comma incorrectly to join two sentences?
options: The bus was late, so we missed the start.
The bus was late, and we missed the start.
Because the bus was late, we missed the start.
The bus was late, we missed the start.
questions.why: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences. You need a full stop or a joining word such as "so" or "and".

questions.prompt: Which sentence puts commas round extra information correctly?
options: Maya, who lives nearby, walks to college.
Maya who lives nearby, walks to college.
Maya, who lives nearby walks to college.
Maya who, lives nearby walks to college.
questions.why: Extra information in the middle goes between a pair of commas.

questions.prompt: Which sentence punctuates the person being spoken to correctly?
options: Thank you Mr, Patel for your reply.
Thank you, Mr Patel, for your reply.
Thank, you Mr Patel for your reply.
Thank you Mr Patel, for, your reply.
questions.why: The name of the person you are addressing goes between commas.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has commas round "in my opinion"?
options: The bus in my opinion is, better value.
The, bus in my opinion, is better value.
The bus in, my opinion is better value.
The bus, in my opinion, is better value.
questions.why: A phrase such as "in my opinion" in the middle of a sentence is set off by commas.

questions.prompt: Which sentence punctuates a list of describing words correctly?
options: It was a long, hot, tiring walk.
It was a long hot, tiring, walk.
It was a, long hot tiring walk.
It was a long, hot tiring, walk.
questions.why: Describing words in a list are separated by commas.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has a comma after "Firstly"?
options: Firstly I would, like to ask about prices.
Firstly I would like, to ask about prices.
Firstly, I would like to ask about prices.
Firstly I would like to ask, about prices.
questions.why: A comma follows an opening word like "Firstly".

spag.name: Apostrophes for belonging
explain: Use an apostrophe to show something belongs to someone: "the keeper's talk" (one keeper).
If the owner is a plural ending in s, put the apostrophe after the s: "the pandas' enclosure" (more than one panda).
Plurals that don't own anything don't need an apostrophe: "two pandas", not "two panda's".

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
questions.why: The seat belongs to one driver, so it is "driver's". "Buses" is just a plural, so it never needs an apostrophe.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct if one girl owns the bag?
questions.why: For one owner, the apostrophe goes before the s.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct if several girls own the bags?
questions.why: For a plural ending in s, the apostrophe goes after the s.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has no apostrophe error?
options: Two bus's arrived at the stop.
Two buses' arrived at the stop.
Two buse's arrived at the stop.
Two buses arrived at the stop.
questions.why: "Buses" is just a plural. Nothing belongs to the buses, so no apostrophe is needed.

questions.prompt: Which is correct for the ears of several pandas?
questions.why: Several pandas, so the apostrophe goes after the s.

questions.prompt: Which shows that the games belong to the children?
questions.why: "Children" is already plural without an s, so the apostrophe goes before an added s.

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows that the letter belongs to Mr Patel?
questions.why: The letter belongs to Mr Patel, so add 's.

questions.prompt: Which is correct for the library that belongs to one college?
options: The college's library is open late.
The colleges library is open late.
The college library's is open late.
The colleges' library is open late.
questions.why: One college owns the library, so the apostrophe goes before the s.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has an apostrophe error?
questions.why: "Tickets" is a plural, but nothing belongs to the tickets in this sentence.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct way to write the work of one day?
questions.why: The work belongs to one day, so the apostrophe goes before the s.

spag.name: Apostrophes for missing letters
explain: An apostrophe can show where letters have been left out: "don't" (do not), "we're" (we are), "it's" (it is).
"Its" without an apostrophe means "belonging to it": "The bus changed its route."
In formal writing, such as a report or a formal letter, it is often better to write the full words: "do not" instead of "don't".

example.wrong: Its a long walk and the hill has it's own bus stop.
example.right: It's a long walk and the hill has its own bus stop.

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
options: The village has it's own shop.
questions.why: "It's going to rain" means "it is going to rain", so it needs the apostrophe. In the other sentences, "its" means "belonging to it" and should have no apostrophe.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
questions.why: "They're" is short for "they are".

questions.prompt: Which is the correct short form of "do not"?
questions.why: The apostrophe goes where the "o" has been left out.

questions.prompt: Which word completes the sentence correctly? "The bus changed ___ route."
questions.why: "Its" without an apostrophe means "belonging to it".

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the short forms of "we are" and "did not" correctly?
options: Were late because the train didnt arrive.
We're late because the train didn't arrive.
We're late because the train did'nt arrive.
We'er late because the train didn't arrive.
questions.why: "We're" is "we are" and "didn't" is "did not", with the apostrophe where the letter is missing.

questions.prompt: Which sentence asks who something belongs to, correctly?
questions.why: "Whose" asks who something belongs to. "Who's" means "who is".

questions.prompt: Which is most suitable for a formal letter?
options: I do not agree with the proposal.
I don't agree with the proposal.
I dont agree with the proposal.
I do'nt agree with the proposal.
questions.why: Formal writing usually avoids short forms.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the short form of "I would" correctly?
questions.why: "I'd" is short for "I would".

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses "you're" correctly?
options: Your going to love the food.
Youre going to love the food.
You'r going to love the food.
You're going to love the food.
questions.why: "You're" means "you are".

questions.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Thats the café where weve eaten before.
That's the café where we've eaten before.
That's the café where we'ave eaten before.
Thats' the café where we've eaten before.
questions.why: "That's" is "that is" and "we've" is "we have".

spag.name: Inverted commas (speech marks)
explain: Put inverted commas around the exact words someone said: The keeper said, "Pandas like a quiet space."
The punctuation at the end of the spoken words goes inside the inverted commas.
You can also use inverted commas around a short quotation or a title: the council calls it "a better route".

example.wrong: The driver said "next stop, Station Road".
example.right: The driver said, "Next stop, Station Road."

questions.prompt: Which is punctuated correctly?
options: My friend said "the train is quicker".
My friend said, The train is "quicker."
My friend said, "The train is quicker."
"My friend said", the train is quicker.
questions.why: There is a comma before the speech, the spoken words start with a capital letter, and the full stop goes inside the inverted commas.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The keeper said "Please keep your voice low".
The keeper said, "please keep your voice low."
The keeper said, Please keep your voice low.
The keeper said, "Please keep your voice low."
questions.why: There is a comma before the speech, the spoken sentence starts with a capital, and the full stop is inside the inverted commas.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses inverted commas correctly for a short quotation?
options: The council calls the new route "a better service".
The council calls the new route a better service".
The council calls the "new route a better service.
The council "calls" the new route a better service.
questions.why: The inverted commas go round exactly the words quoted.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct for a spoken question?
options: She asked, "Where is the nearest stop"?
She asked, "Where is the nearest stop?"
She asked "Where is the nearest stop?".
She asked, Where is the "nearest stop?"
questions.why: The question mark belongs to the spoken question, so it goes inside the inverted commas.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has split speech punctuated correctly?
options: "I would, said Dani, like a window seat."
"I would" said Dani "like a window seat."
"I would, said Dani", "like a window seat."
"I would," said Dani, "like a window seat."
questions.why: Each part of the speech has its own inverted commas, and commas separate the speech from "said Dani".

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives the speaker's exact words and so needs inverted commas?
options: Priya said, "Pandas are happiest when there is plenty to climb."
Priya said that pandas are happiest when there is plenty to climb.
Priya said pandas are happiest when there is plenty to climb.
questions.why: Inverted commas show the exact words spoken. The others report them indirectly.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has the punctuation in the right place?
questions.why: The full stop belongs to the spoken sentence, so it goes inside.

questions.prompt: When a new person starts speaking, what should you do?
questions.why: A new speaker gets a new line, which makes dialogue easy to follow.

questions.prompt: Which sentence quotes the text correctly?
options: The writer says that buses are slow, noisy and old-fashioned".
The writer says that buses are "slow, noisy and old-fashioned".
The writer says that "buses are slow, noisy and old-fashioned.
The writer says that buses are "slow, noisy and old-fashioned.
questions.why: Both opening and closing inverted commas are needed, round exactly the words quoted.

questions.prompt: Which sentence punctuates speech followed by "said Maya" correctly?
questions.why: A comma, not a full stop, goes inside the closing inverted commas before "said Maya".

spag.name: Words that sound the same
explain: "There" is a place (over there). "Their" means belonging to them. "They're" means they are.
"Your" means belonging to you. "You're" means you are.
"To" is for direction (to the bus stop). "Too" means also or very (too late). "Two" is the number 2.

example.wrong: Their going too the station at to o'clock.
example.right: They're going to the station at two o'clock.

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
options: Your going to love the food.
Youre going to love the food.
Your' going to love the food.
You're going to love the food.
questions.why: "You're" is short for "you are": "You are going to love the food."

questions.prompt: Which word completes the sentence? "___ going to arrive at six."
questions.why: "They're" means "they are".

questions.prompt: Which word completes the sentence? "It was ___ hot to walk."
questions.why: "Too" means "very" or "more than is wanted".

questions.prompt: Which word completes the sentence? "The weather will ___ our plans."
questions.why: "Affect" is the verb meaning "to change or influence".

questions.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of the word meaning "for certain"?
questions.why: Remember "finite" in the middle: de-finite-ly.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of the word meaning "apart"?
questions.why: There is "a rat" in sep-a-rate.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct way to write the phrase meaning "many"?
questions.why: "A lot" is two words.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of the word meaning "to get"?
questions.why: "I before E, except after C."

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses "whether" and "weather" correctly?
options: I wonder whether the weather will be good.
I wonder weather the whether will be good.
I wonder whether the whether will be good.
I wonder weather the weather will be good.
questions.why: "Whether" means "if". "Weather" is about rain and sunshine.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of the word meaning "a place to stay"?
questions.why: It has a double c and a double m.

spag.name: Grammar: was or were, and staying in one tense
explain: Use "was" with I, he, she and it. Use "were" with we, you and they: "We were late."
Pick a tense and stick to it. If you start in the past ("we went"), keep going in the past ("we saw", not "we see").
Write "should have" or "could have", not "should of" or "could of".

example.wrong: We was on the train and then we see the sea.
example.right: We were on the train and then we saw the sea.

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
options: They were waiting at the stop.
Yesterday we go to the park.
questions.why: "They" goes with "were". The others mix up was and were, use "should of" instead of "should have", or use the wrong tense for yesterday.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the right tense for yesterday?
options: Yesterday we visit the market and bought some olives.
Yesterday we visited the market and bought some olives.
Yesterday we visited the market and buy some olives.
Yesterday we visiting the market and bought olives.
questions.why: Both verbs are in the past tense.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses "doesn't" correctly?
questions.why: "She" goes with "doesn't", and the main verb stays in its base form.

questions.prompt: Which uses "a" and "an" correctly?
questions.why: "An" goes before a vowel sound and "a" before a consonant sound.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses "should have" correctly?
questions.why: It is always "should have", never "should of".

questions.prompt: Which word completes the sentence? "The bus and the train ___ both late."
questions.why: Two things joined by "and" take the plural verb "were".

questions.prompt: Which sentence keeps the same tense all the way through?
options: I opened the door, look outside and saw the bus.
I opened the door, looked outside and saw the bus.
I open the door, looked outside and saw the bus.
I opened the door, looked outside and see the bus.
questions.why: All three verbs are in the past tense.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses "fewer" correctly?
options: There are fewer buses on Sundays.
There are less buses on Sundays.
There is fewer buses on Sundays.
There are lesser buses on Sundays.
questions.why: Use "fewer" for things you can count, such as buses.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct when two people went to the zoo?
options: Me and my friend went to the zoo.
My friend and me went to the zoo.
My friend and I went to the zoo.
I and my friend goes to the zoo.
questions.why: Try it with "I" alone: "I went to the zoo." So "My friend and I" is right.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses "good" and "well" correctly?
options: She writes good and has well ideas.
She writes good and has good ideas.
She writes well and has well ideas.
She writes well and has good ideas.
questions.why: "Well" describes how she writes (an adverb), and "good" describes the ideas (an adjective).
